lesson.title: G, CH & Dutch Spelling
lesson.subtitle: yellow → geel, year → jaar, and the t that turns back into d

hook.title: Yellow, Good — and the Disappearing D
hook.content: English y often answers to Dutch g in words like yellow → geel and yield → gelden, but year → jaar takes Dutch j. The letters are close; the sound is not always the same. And Dutch has a spelling law English lost: a final consonant may sound voiceless while the spelling keeps the voiced letter. Hond sounds like hont, but the plural honden brings the d back.

pattern.title: Write the underlying consonant
pattern.content: Dutch writes the consonant that returns when the word grows: hond → honden, huis → huizen, stad → steden. The final sound may devoice, but the spelling remembers the family. Year/jaar is a y↔j twin, not a y↔g one; keep the two families separate.
pattern.linguist_note: Final devoicing is a regular Dutch process; the orthography keeps the voiced consonant so the plural remains transparent.
pattern.trap_note: Do not write what you hear at the end of a word. If the plural has d, the singular keeps d even when it sounds like t.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (G, CH & Dutch Spelling):
exercises.target_answer: geel, het jaar, goed, de hond, de stad, het huis
exercises.meaning: yellow, year, good, dog, city, house
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "G, CH & Dutch Spelling": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The dog is small.”?
exercises.explanation: “De hond is klein.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “G, CH & Dutch Spelling”.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not write what you hear at the end of a word. If the plural has d, the singular keeps d even when it sounds like t.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Het huis is geel.” is word-for-word “The house is yellow.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Write the underlying consonant.

cues: It means: The year is long.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The city is old.”
twist.explanation: Stad ends in a d that sounds like t; the plural steden restores it.

foreshadow.line: You now have the decode engine. The next stretch turns it into a sentence machine — starting with the two verbs every Dutch sentence leans on.

summary.outcome: Match y↔g and y↔j twins and spell Dutch final consonants by their plural, not by their sound.
summary.takeaway: Dutch spelling is morphological: the word's family decides the letter.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Final Devoicing Gym.

geel.etymology_derivation: English yellow and Dutch geel are cognate; English y answers to Dutch g here.

jaar.etymology_derivation: English year and Dutch jaar are the same word; both take a y/j, not a g.

goed.etymology_derivation: English good and Dutch goed are the same word.

hond.etymology_derivation: English hound and Dutch hond are the same word; the final d devoices.

stad.etymology_derivation: English stead and Dutch stad are the same word; Dutch narrowed it to city.

huis.etymology_derivation: English house and Dutch huis are the same word; ui answers to ou.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.
